title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)
summary: Defines the Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR), a binary data format designed for very small code size, fairly small messages and extensibility without version negotiation. It differs from earlier binary formats such as ASN.1 and MessagePack. It has been replaced by RFC 8949.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to write down information in a very compact secret-shorthand that small gadgets can read quickly.

subtitle: A compact binary format for small devices and simple messages

tldr.problem: Network devices with very limited memory and processing power need a way to send structured data to each other, but existing binary formats like ASN.1 are too large and complex to implement, and text formats like JSON are inefficient for constrained devices.
tldr.mechanism: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) uses a simple encoding where each value starts with a type indicator (the first three bits) and size information (the last five bits), followed by the value itself. Major types cover integers, byte strings, text strings, arrays, maps, and optional semantic tags. The format is self-describing, so a decoder does not need a schema.
tldr.outcome: CBOR has become widely deployed in IoT and constrained-device applications. RFC 8949 obsoleted and refined this RFC to clarify security considerations and improve the specification.

facts.label: Major types
facts.value: 7 (types 0-6; type 7 for floats and simple values)

facts.label: Initial byte information
facts.value: 3 bits for major type, 5 bits for additional data

today: RFC 7049 is a Proposed Standard (later Standards Track) published in October 2013. It was obsoleted by RFC 8949 in December 2020, which clarified security considerations, improved the specification, and made minor editorial improvements. However, the core CBOR encoding and concepts remain the same. CBOR has seen significant adoption in IoT, constrained-device applications, and protocols requiring compact serialization.

sections.title: Small Code, Small Messages, No Schema Needed
sections.content:
CBOR was designed with three priorities: extremely small encoder and decoder implementations, reasonably small message size, and the ability for a decoder to understand a message without a schema or prior negotiation. This makes it suitable for resource-constrained devices like sensors, embedded systems, and IoT gateways that cannot afford the memory footprint of format negotiation, schema parsers, or large codec implementations.

CBOR extends the JSON data model by adding byte strings (not just text strings) and other constructs, while remaining simple enough to decode in a few kilobytes of code. The design prioritizes code compactness over message compactness: the format uses contemporary machine representations (like native integers) rather than requiring conversions.
sections.plainLanguage: A tiny computer can decode it with only a small program, and it does not need to be told what format the message is in advance. The message itself says what everything is.

sections.title: Seven Major Types in One Initial Byte
sections.content:
Every CBOR value begins with an initial byte that encodes both the type and size information. The first three bits (high-order) identify the major type, and the last five bits give additional information such as the length or the value itself.

Major types 0 and 1 are unsigned and negative integers. Major type 0 encodes non-negative integers; values 0 through 23 fit in the five-bit field itself, and larger values use the additional information to indicate a 1-, 2-, 4-, or 8-byte encoding. Major type 1 encodes negative integers using the same method, with the value being -1 minus the encoded unsigned value.

Major types 2 and 3 are byte strings and UTF-8 text strings. The five-bit field or following bytes indicate the length in bytes, followed by the raw bytes (or UTF-8 text) themselves.

Major types 4 and 5 are arrays and maps. The length field indicates the number of items (for arrays) or key-value pairs (for maps), followed by the encoded items.

Major type 6 provides optional semantic tags that add meaning to values without changing their structure. For example, a tag can mark a byte string as a bignum or a text string as a date.

Major type 7 includes floating-point numbers (16-bit, 32-bit, 64-bit) and simple values like true, false, null, and undefined.
sections.plainLanguage: The first number in each message tells you what kind of thing follows and how big it is. Integers, text, lists and dictionaries are all marked differently, so the decoder knows what to do.

sections.title: Tags and Semantic Extensions
sections.content:
While the core CBOR encoding is complete by itself, semantic tags (major type 6) allow additional meaning to be attached to values. A tag is identified by a number and precedes a single data item. The same underlying value is transmitted, but the tag indicates how the decoder should interpret it.

For example, tag 0 marks a UTF-8 string as a date in RFC 3339 format; tag 1 marks an integer or float as the number of seconds since the Unix epoch; tags 2 and 3 mark byte strings as bignums (very large integers). Tags 21, 22, and 23 hint that a byte string might be encoded as base64url, base64, or hex when converting to JSON. The IANA maintains a registry of tag values, so future applications can define new semantic meanings without conflicting with existing ones.

Critically, decoders that do not understand a tag can still decode the underlying data item; the tag is optional information. This allows forward compatibility: a new CBOR message with an unknown tag can still be decoded by an old decoder that simply ignores the tag.
sections.plainLanguage: You can attach a note to a value to say what it really means—for example, 'this number is a date' or 'this byte string is really a huge number.' Old decoders ignore the note and just read the value anyway.

sections.title: Indefinite Lengths for Streaming
sections.content:
Most CBOR values have a definite length encoded upfront: you know how many array items follow, how many bytes the string contains. However, CBOR also supports indefinite-length arrays, maps, and strings using additional information value 31. An indefinite-length array or map opens with major type 4 or 5 and additional information 31, followed by the items. A special "break" marker (major type 7, additional information 31) signals the end.

Indefinite-length strings work differently: they are a sequence of definite-length chunks of the same major type, followed by the break code. For example, an indefinite-length byte string is zero or more definite-length byte strings concatenated together. This is useful in streaming applications where the total length is not known upfront, allowing the encoder to begin transmission before collecting all data.
sections.plainLanguage: For very long things, you can start sending chunks before you know how many chunks there will be. A special "stop" signal tells the decoder you are done.

sections.title: How It Compares to JSON and Other Formats
sections.content:
CBOR extends JSON's data model: anything you can encode in JSON (numbers, strings, arrays, objects) can be encoded in CBOR, and conversion between them is straightforward. However, CBOR adds byte strings and is far more compact on the wire: a small integer takes 1 byte in CBOR but multiple bytes as ASCII text in JSON. Text strings are UTF-8 encoded bytes rather than escaped sequences.

Unlike ASN.1 (a complex binary format developed for telecom), CBOR is far simpler and requires little code to implement. Compared to MessagePack (another binary format), CBOR's design prioritizes code size over message size and includes semantic tagging for extensibility. For constrained devices, the small encoder and decoder footprint matters more than squeezing the last byte from messages.

CBOR is designed to be decodable without a schema, unlike many other binary formats that require the decoder to know the structure in advance. This makes CBOR suitable for generic codec implementations and gives it flexibility for protocols that evolve over time.
sections.plainLanguage: It is smaller than JSON for the same information, simpler to program than older binary formats, and does not need you to say in advance what shape the data is.
